note: B covers activities, coaching and a suitable audience. A omits evaluation and C changes subject. Feedback properly avoids prescribing a paragraph count.
Suitability for younger viewers is the aim, not popularity or a genre comparison. Retain the distinctions in feedback and ask what younger viewers will want to know.
A addresses students choosing a meetup. B addresses owners and C narrows the purpose to the menu. Replace “identify the purpose most closely” with a direct question about the review’s purpose.

C uniquely assesses beginner suitability, but “must include” could also lead learners to expect the second requirement, a gameplay description. Ask which judgement meets the beginner requirement. Feedback should say both requirements still apply.
Only B links price to included hands-on activity. A lacks evidence about what entry buys and C names extras. Feedback correctly treats price plus benefits as evidence rather than proof for everyone.
Demonstration plus feedback provides direct support. Worksheets and a finished example may also help, which the feedback acknowledges. Good evidence comparison at Bronze.

Repeated clues provide the strongest evidence of slow narrative progress; running time and short scenes may also inform other judgements about pace. Specify the claim that the middle felt slow so those plausible alternatives address the same decision.
The observed five-minute service directly addresses time. Discounts relate to price and advance orders do not establish service speed. Feedback does not claim that the entire trip fits.

A alone covers premise, acting, pace and audience. “Manageable” implies a limit that the item does not state, and the other plans leave out different requirements. Give the word target and compare complete plans with different levels of plot detail.

C best supports value and audience, but “two meal prices and portions” may fulfil food description only if the actual foods are named. State both dishes in the plan and include an explicit value judgement. Keep partially relevant alternatives.

B is intended, but explaining how signs affected queues does not establish what arrival time follows. Add the actual queue observation and resulting advice, or specify the plan must show that connection. A and C currently already miss it.

A is the strongest content plan. The word range is unstated and the second option is broadly relevant but inefficient. Supply 120–160 words and a practical contrast between short-chapter evidence and extended summary.
The targeted recommendation fills a missing brief point using existing evidence. Wording and more facilities evidence can wait. Clear constrained choice; do not present it as a universal priority.
Cutting repetition retains useful evidence and the recommendation. B and C protect repetition at the expense of different relevant content. The advice is framed as revision within a word target.

The short, easy mystery directly supports a narrower audience. Additional introduction detail and exact duration are potentially useful but leave the approval broad. Feedback balances these priorities.

C addresses the stated readability issue whereas A and B add or redistribute content. Let learners choose between edits to actual sentences and avoid implying every long sentence has faulty boundaries.
B covers teaching and audience. Materials and artwork can support but do not satisfy the brief independently. Good checkpoint opening linked to a single scenario.

The demonstration before practice is the strongest evidence. Materials and examples are plausible lesser support. This repeats Bronze workshop selection; combine with the other art-course items into a single independent planning decision.

A addresses the missing audience and grounds advice in teaching. The other edits may improve detail or enthusiasm but keep the broad ending. To test transfer, ask for an actual targeted recommendation using evidence from the preceding art-course step.

The second opening names the experience and offers an initial judgement. Ask learners to select it and identify the two features separately. Give the school-reader purpose clearly to avoid another generic opinion prompt.
Value is missing from the shorter noodle example. Check that explicitly, then compare how the price and portion develop value. Three words can satisfy the gate without identifying the omission.

The charging-point example gives a reason relevant to people waiting for a train. Name that reader in the prompt. Compare the usefulness of breadth and depth rather than treating lists as always inadequate.

The second accommodates budget constraints and motives. Check price, equipment and beneficiary separately, then allow optional short audience advice. The note rightly distinguishes tone from reader-focused content.

The second version is clearer but supplies back seats, view and every line beyond the vague first version. Add those observations to a common source before teaching that the revision preserves meaning. Check usable language rather than word length.

The birthday sets a social purpose for mood and welcome, but the stem implies all readers need the birthday itself. Compare a relevant social introduction with an unrelated one and explain why a brief context helps.

Display the actual brief when asking students to match content. Sandwiches and cake describe food and “reasonably priced” evaluates cost without a number. Match both links and explain the different functions.

The prompt asks about balance. Pair drinks delay with food and crowding with welcome or the quiet corner. Check evidence links rather than requiring six words. Model balance without teaching that every review must give equal space to both sides.
The audience and timing are directly identifiable. Use a quick matching check; show the earlier crowding only if asking why the advice works. Make optional after Willow’s similar audience exercise.
Lunch after badminton explains the visit; several meals under ¥40 help a reader consider cost. Ask each separately and check those links, including that “several” does not mean all meals.

Several pairs of food details are defensible; the note recognises this. Retain a short open response and self-review whether each selected detail explains the experience. Avoid a single best pair or a length-only completion signal.
The wait matters to hurried students; music matters to those wanting conversation. A checked evidence/reader-needs match makes the rationale visible and avoids duplicating a generic explanation task.

Show the earlier queue and noise when requiring evidence from elsewhere. The two audiences can overlap. Match price and portion to hunger/budget and timing to conversation without implying early visits guarantee quiet.

The separation sets up the premise without revealing an outcome. Show the relevant brief, then compare this opening with a plausible overlong summary. The response should assess sufficiency for the task rather than count words.
The arguments show a realistic relationship and conversations explain its depth. Ask which detail supports which judgement, using the strength requirement openly. Avoid generic length scoring.
The station search is about the slow middle and the soundtrack strengthens the ending. Ask which detail supports which judgement. “Blanket judgement” adds an idiom without clarifying the scope test.
The two audience groups are explicit. Ask learners to select an ending for a named viewer profile; make optional if the Idea Development recommendation work already establishes the distinction.
The map and photographer establish the premise briefly. Use a contrast with a longer opening and a named word budget. Combine with Beyond the Stars or use one as optional independent practice.

Pair markets and villages with setting praise, and similar minor characters with dialogue difficulty. Show the brief’s evaluative requirement. This is a concrete check rather than a generic written response.

The earlier weakness is absent from the shown paragraph and omitted from the feedback. Include the earlier sentence and ask how the writer balances confusion with short chapters and discoveries. Do not equate accessible adventure with a requirement to mention historical novels.

The local young musicians and visit with classmates establish relevance. Match what identifies the festival and what helps school readers connect with it. Make opening-purpose practice optional where duplicated.

Examples are grouped by what happens on stage versus between concerts. Feedback currently lists them without explaining that grouping. Check which summary preserves both groups without overloading the opening.
The audience's dancing and the discomfort in the heat are evidence for opposing judgements. Have learners distinguish evidence from evaluation for each without a length gate.

Price and what is included are missing; the wording implies a price fact exists in the extract. Ask what fact is missing and show earlier activities if learners must judge benefits. The note acknowledges the price gap and should ground any advice in named evidence.

Opening names activity and range of experience levels, while the question invites readers seeking a free afternoon. Clarify that “free” is available time, not free entry. Use a checked audience/content link.
Low course and zip line are descriptions; demonstration and increased confidence support evaluation. Match excerpts to their function. “Facilities” is less direct than “activities” here.

Equipment and repeat attempts at most courses qualify cost and food is a separate budget consideration. Check both constraints. Unlike the festival, the model supplies what the admission covers but still gives no exact price.

The café limitation is needed to justify the lunch advice. The morning booking may be practical but has no specific reason in the extracts. Show the café evidence and do not require students to justify morning timing without facts.
Robot, tools and puzzles show basic gameplay without rules. Compare a task-focused premise with detailed mechanics, or make this optional after the film and book openings.

The magnets and platforms show how tools are combined to reach places. Clarify whether learners are linking this to puzzle design or enjoyment. Do not assume the extract establishes exactly when each skill was taught.

The criticism concerns some advanced instructions and repeated actions by inexperienced players. Select the resulting limitation instead of implying the entire game is unsuitable. Feedback should retain the proposed tutorial as hypothetical.

Puzzle preference and short sessions are separate selling points. Ask which evidence supports each reader need and make optional alongside the same passage’s other lenses. Do not exclude all players interested in scores.
The opening compares experiments with textbooks and states the writer’s view. Check which judgement the review needs to support. A restatement is insufficient for assessing independent exam planning.

Bridge, light and robot examples show activities, but specific learning outcomes are mostly left implicit. Ask which facts show what students did and which evaluate access, retaining beginner-friendly explanations and crowding.
Separate suggested audience from weekday timing and show earlier crowding evidence if requesting the link. Keep benefits as observed/believed rather than assuming every weekday is quiet.

The open plan meets the minimum and covers a robot activity, teaching and a limitation, but notes mostly name facts without showing the two opinions requested. Model explicit judgement/evidence pairs and clarify the 120–160 range applies to the eventual response, not the plan.

The plan includes tuition and material costs but lacks an actual price or a clear value judgement and gives little link from beginner support to the recommendation. Include those notes and distinguish the internal eight-word gate from evidence of a usable plan.

The original practice model fits the target and develops food, seating and relative value for students. Quietness by the window is inferred rather than observed. Phrase the seat advice as a possibility. Keep the four review passes as self-review and make one check specific to the required seating point.

The practice review fits the target and develops acting and pace without spoilers. The soundtrack sentence adds an undeveloped third aspect. Remove or connect it to an existing point. Use the broad checklist to check the two required aspects and spoiler-free synopsis.

The review fits the range and links an activity, clear directions and crowding to how easy it is to learn. It recommends the museum for a specific group and offers proportionate advice. The review passes support self-review, and the practice submission warning is separate from scoring.

The mock model fits the range, covers varied food, price and portion, and targets readers with differing budgets and tastes. Advice follows the queue and seating limitations. The shared review passes are relevant and function as self-review.

The mock response fits the target, supports praise with comic timing and pairs a clear sound problem with a practical improvement. Its recommendation identifies students seeking an accessible evening. Keep the timer labelled as Hub practice and the checklist as reflection.

The mock model fits the range, explains cooperation and offers an example of how quieter players can contribute. The half-hour suitability appears only in the verdict. Include an observed round length or qualify the time. Use the checks to inspect that evidence link.

The response fits the range and shows step-by-step repair learning. It states that working in pairs was enjoyable without explaining why. Develop one specific cooperative detail and retain the qualified pump drawback and targeted advice. Use the checklist as self-review.
